- How do I organize my work for this lesson?
- How do I get the data used in this lesson?

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: objectives

- Create an RStudio project with a folder for the data.
- Download the lesson data.
- Check that the required packages are installed.

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

## Create an RStudio project

It is good practice to keep all files of one analysis in one folder. An
**RStudio project** helps with this: when you open the project, R
automatically uses the project folder as its *working directory*. All file
paths in this lesson are relative to this folder.

1. In RStudio, choose *File* → *New Project* → *New Directory* → *New Project*.
2. Name the project `microbiome-lesson` and choose where to save it.
3. Click *Create Project*.

Next, create a folder called `data` inside the project for the input files.
You can use the *New Folder* button in the *Files* pane, or run:

```{r create-dirs, eval=FALSE}
dir.create("data")
```

Finally, open a new R script (*File* → *New File* → *R Script*) and save it
in the project folder, for example as `microbiome-analysis.R`. Write the code
of the following episodes into this script, so that you can run it again
later.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: prereq

## New to R and RStudio?

This lesson assumes you know the basics of R and RStudio. If you need a
refresher, see the
[Introduction to data analysis with R and Bioconductor](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/bioc-intro/)
lesson.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

## Download the data

The data consists of the four parts of a microbiome dataset (see
[episode 1](01-intro-microbiome.Rmd)), each in its own file:

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `taxonomy_abundance.csv` | Abundance table: taxa × samples |
| `taxonomy_table.csv` | Taxonomy of each taxon |
| `sample_metadata.csv` | Information about each sample |
| `phylogeny.tree` | Phylogenetic tree of the taxa |

We download them into the `data` folder with `download.file()`. Here is the
first one:

```{r download-first, eval=FALSE}
download.file(
    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microbiome/microbiome-lesson/main/episodes/data/taxonomy_abundance.csv",
    destfile = file.path("data", "taxonomy_abundance.csv")
)
```

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: callout

## File paths with `file.path()`

The function `file.path()` joins folder and file names into a path:
`file.path("data", "taxonomy_abundance.csv")` gives
`"data/taxonomy_abundance.csv"`. Forward slashes work on Windows, macOS and
Linux alike, but `file.path()` saves you from typing the separators yourself,
so we use it for all file paths in this lesson.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: challenge

## Challenge 1: Download the other files

Download the remaining three files (`taxonomy_table.csv`,
`sample_metadata.csv` and `phylogeny.tree`) into the `data` folder. Then
check that all four files are there.

:::::::::::::::::::::::: solution

```{r download-rest, eval=FALSE}
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microbiome/microbiome-lesson/main/episodes/data/"

download.file(paste0(url, "taxonomy_table.csv"), file.path("data", "taxonomy_table.csv"))
download.file(paste0(url, "sample_metadata.csv"), file.path("data", "sample_metadata.csv"))
download.file(paste0(url, "phylogeny.tree"), file.path("data", "phylogeny.tree"))

list.files("data")
```

## Check the packages

We use these packages:

| Package | Used for | Episodes |
|---|---|---|
| **mia** | Microbiome analysis | all |
| **miaViz** | Microbiome visualization | all |
| **ape** | Reading the phylogenetic tree | 4 |
| **scater** | Principal component analysis (PCA) | 7 |
| **bluster** | Clustering | 7, 10 |
| **daa** | Simple statistical tests (Wilcoxon test, t-test, linear model) | 5, 6, 8 |
| **maaslin3** | Differential abundance and prevalence | 8, 10 |
| **mikropml** | Machine learning | 9 |

mia, miaViz and daa belong to the OMA framework. Each episode loads the packages
it needs with `library()`.

If you followed the [setup instructions](../learners/setup.md), the packages
are already installed. Check that they load without errors:

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(ape)
library(scater)
library(bluster)
library(maaslin3)
library(mikropml)
```

We do not load the daa package with `library()`. Instead, we call its
functions with `daa::` in front, as in `daa::getLm()`. Check that it is
installed by asking for its version:

```{r check-daa}
packageVersion("daa")
```

Messages are normal. If you see an error such as
`there is no package called 'mia'`, go back to the
[setup instructions](../learners/setup.md).

::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::: keypoints

- Use an RStudio project to keep the data, code and results of an analysis together.
- Use `download.file()` to download data from the internet, and `file.path()` to build file paths.
- The main packages of this lesson are mia and miaViz from the OMA framework; later episodes also use ape, scater, bluster, daa, maaslin3 and mikropml.
